text.en: In Shimla people wear sweaters in May while in Chennai they sip cool drinks. People say, it is very hot today, but that is weather, not climate. Climate is the pattern of weather over many years. In this chapter we ask what makes India's climate so diverse and how it shapes our lives.

Weather changes from day to day. Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period, usually 30 years or more. Each season lasts a few months and recurs every year. Most regions have four seasons: spring (vasanta), summer, autumn (sharad) and winter, and trees bloom or shed leaves and some animals grow thick fur according to the season.
Latitude: the angle at which the sun's rays strike an area. Places near the equator are hot and those near the poles are cold. India has a tropical climate in the south and a subtropical climate in the northern plains, with very hot summers and cold winters. Altitude: temperature falls as we climb, so hill stations in mountains are cool. The Himalayas are so high that many peaks stay below freezing and are snow-covered. Distance from the sea: coastal places have a moderate climate, with small differences between summer and winter. As you move inland the climate becomes more extreme, with hotter summers and colder winters. Winds: dry winds from deserts bring dry conditions, while winds from the sea carry moisture and bring rain. The Himalayas and Karakoram protect India to some extent from the cold dry winds of Central Asia. A microclimate is the climate of a small area that differs from the region around it, such as a garden or a valley.
The monsoon is central to life in India. As summer begins the Asian landmass heats up and a strong low-pressure area forms over it. Moist winds from the Indian Ocean rush in towards the land and bring heavy rain, the south-west monsoon. In winter the winds reverse and blow from the land to the sea. They are dry and cold, but a part passes over the Bay of Bengal, picks up moisture and brings rain to parts of east and south India, such as Tamil Nadu. Predicting monsoon rainfall has always been important, and our ancestors observed Nature carefully to do so.
Our food, clothes, houses, festivals, songs and work are all tied to climate. Farmers depend on the monsoon, and many festivals celebrate the harvest. Climate disasters strain life. Heavy rain can cause floods and landslides, especially in hilly regions like Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. An intense low-pressure system with high winds can become a cyclone, and the areas around the Kedarnath temple were destroyed by floods in 2013. The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is specially trained to respond to natural and human-made disasters.
Climate change means significant long-term changes in climate. A natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life, but burning fossil fuels such as coal and oil adds more greenhouse gases and warms the planet further. A warmer planet means problems for farming and for small industries, so we must reduce the causes by saving energy, planting trees and using cleaner energy.

problem.en: Why is Shimla cooler than Delhi even though both are in north India?

text.en: Shimla is in the mountains at a higher altitude.
Delhi is in the plains and far from the sea, so it is more extreme.
So Shimla is cooler in summer.

prompt.en: Explain how latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and winds affect climate.

requiredIdeas.en: Latitude: sun's angle, hot near the equator.
Sea distance and winds: coast moderate, inland extreme, winds bring moisture.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the monsoon blows in only one direction.

points.en: Climate is the long-term pattern of weather.
Latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and winds decide climate.
The monsoon brings most of India's rain.
Climate change is a long-term warming we must slow.
